passages.happening:
Paul goes on explaining why he did not come back to Corinth. He had decided against it: “So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you” (verse 1).

The reason was love, not coldness. If he came and grieved them again, who would be left to cheer him? Only the people he had hurt (verse 2).

So he wrote instead. He wanted things put right before he came, so that his next visit would be a joy and not a sorrow (verse 3).

Then Paul tells them how that letter was written. “For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
‘Another painful visit’ tells us there had already been one. Acts does not mention it. But Paul later speaks of coming to Corinth ‘the third time’ (13:1). The first visit was when he started the church. The second, it seems, went badly. Someone in the church seems to have wronged Paul or opposed him openly, and the church did not take his side at first (see 7:12).

The letter Paul wrote afterwards is often called the tearful letter. What became of it is not known. Many think it is lost. Some think part of it survives in chapters 10 to 13 of this letter. A few have thought it was 1 Corinthians, though most find that 1 Corinthians does not read like a letter written in tears. These notes do not choose, as the book page says.

Listen to the words Paul uses in four verses: painful, grieve, saddened, rejoice, joy, tears, distress, anguish, love. These are the words of a hurt relationship. Paul is not writing as an official giving orders. He is writing as a father who has had a bitter quarrel with his children and wants them back.

In Corinth people admired leaders who looked calm, strong and in control. Paul tells them he wept as he wrote. He does not think that makes him less of an apostle. Hard words and deep love came from the same heart.
passages.ot:
The prophets wept over the people they warned. Jeremiah cried, “Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people” (Jeremiah 9:1). His hard messages were spoken with grief, not contempt.

The law joined honest rebuke with love. “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him” (Leviticus 19:17). The next verse says, “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). A true rebuke is a form of love, not a break from it.

The proverb says, “The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Proverbs 27:6).

Paul's tears were not new. He reminded the leaders of Ephesus, “for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears” (Acts 20:31).
passages.asks: Paul chose a letter over a visit so that the next meeting could be a joy. Ask whether there is a hard word you need to say to someone, and how you could say it so that they know you love them. And ask whether someone's hard words to you came, like Paul's, from tears rather than anger.

passages.happening:
Now Paul speaks about the man who caused the trouble. “Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you” (verse 5). Paul will not make it only about himself.

The church had punished the man. Paul says it is enough. “The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him” (verse 6).

Now the church must change course. “So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (verse 7). “Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him” (verse 8).

Paul's letter had been a test of whether they would obey (verse 9). Now he joins them in forgiving. “If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him” (verse 10). He has forgiven in Christ's presence, for their sake, “in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Who was this man? Paul does not name him. The Corinthians knew, and we do not.

For a long time many readers thought he was the man of 1 Corinthians 5, who was living with his father's wife and whom Paul told the church to put out of its fellowship. Paul there hoped the man would be saved, and here a man who was punished is to be welcomed back, so the link is natural. Many readers today think instead that he was someone who wronged Paul during the painful visit, perhaps by insulting him in front of the church. They point out that Paul speaks of the grief as done to him in part (verse 5), and later speaks of ‘the one who did wrong’ and ‘the one who was harmed’ (7:12). These notes do not choose. The point of the passage is the same on either view.

‘By the majority’ shows that the church acted together, not by one leader's order. Some may have wanted to go further, or felt the man had not suffered enough.

Paul says stop. The purpose of discipline was never to crush the man. It was to bring him back. Now that he has turned, punishment that goes on would do harm. ‘Overwhelmed’ is literally ‘swallowed up’. Paul uses the same Greek verb for death being swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). Here it is a man who might be swallowed up by grief. Paul does not want the man to sink into despair, or to be lost to the church for good.

The Greek word for ‘forgive’ here comes from the same root as the word for grace. To forgive is to give freely, as God has given.

And Satan's ‘schemes’? Paul does not explain. But the sense is clear. Satan can use a church's sin to harm it. He can also use a church's harshness. A community that will not forgive a person who has turned back has handed the enemy a victory.
passages.ot:
Israel's Scriptures speak of a God who forgives and does not hold anger forever. “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (Psalm 130:3-4). The prophet asks, “Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance” (Micah 7:18).

Joseph is a picture of the comfort Paul asks for. When his brothers, who had sold him, begged him to forgive them, “Joseph wept” (Genesis 50:17). Then he “reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them” (Genesis 50:21).

Jesus taught the same. When Peter asked how many times he should forgive, Jesus answered, “not just seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22). He also said, “If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). Paul's words follow that pattern: a wrong faced, a turning, and then forgiveness and welcome.
passages.hard:
Does this passage mean a church should take back anyone who says sorry, at once and in full, whatever they have done?

Paul's main point is plain. Church discipline aims at restoring a person, not destroying them. When someone has truly turned, the church must forgive, comfort them and show its love again. A church that keeps punishing after that is not being strict. It is being cruel, and Paul says it plays into Satan's hands.

But forgiving a person who has turned is not the same as putting others back in danger. Forgiveness deals with the wrong done. It does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, or giving someone back a position of trust that would put others at risk. The site's note on 1 Corinthians 5:1-5 says it plainly: church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed or to protect someone who has done harm, and abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities. This passage does not change that. Nor does it ask anyone who has been harmed to stay near the person who harmed them, or to act as if they feel safe when they do not.

And notice that the church acted first. The man was not welcomed back while he went on in the wrong. He was welcomed back after he had turned.

If you have been hurt and feel pressed to forgive in a way that would put you or others at risk, that is not what Paul asks. Talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says punishment can go on too long. Ask whether there is someone you have kept at arm's length after they turned and asked to be forgiven. Ask what it would look like to ‘reaffirm your love’ for them. And if you are the one who did wrong and has turned back, hear that Paul did not want such a person overwhelmed by sorrow. There is a way home.

passages.t: Led in triumph, the aroma of Christ
passages.happening:
Paul goes back to his story. He went to Troas to preach, and “a door stood open for me in the Lord” (verse 12). But he could not settle. “I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia” (verse 13).

Then, suddenly, the story stops, and Paul bursts into thanks. “But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him” (verse 14).

He goes on with the picture of a smell. “For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing” (verse 15). To some it smells of death, to others of life. “And who is qualified for such a task?” (verse 16).

Paul ends with a contrast. “For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Troas was a port on the coast of Asia Minor, where travellers crossed by sea to Macedonia in northern Greece. Paul had crossed there before (Acts 16:8-11). Titus was carrying news from Corinth, and Paul was so anxious to hear it that he left an open door for the gospel behind him. It is an honest detail. Paul was not a man without worry.

The story of Titus picks up again in 7:5. Everything in between is Paul's long reflection on what it means to serve Christ.

Verse 14 uses a word from Roman public life. A triumph was a victory parade granted to a winning general. He rode through Rome in a chariot to the temple of Jupiter. His soldiers, the spoils of war and the captives he had taken went with him. Some of the captives, often enemy leaders, were put to death afterwards. Incense burned along the way.

The BSB translates the verb ‘leads us triumphantly as captives’. On that reading, which many hold, Paul pictures himself not as the general but as one of the conquered, led along in Christ's victory parade. Once he had fought against Christ. Now he is Christ's captive, on display for all to see. Others think Paul means that God leads his servants as members of the victory procession, sharing the triumph, not as prisoners. Either way, the victory belongs to God, not to Paul. And it fits what Paul will say all through this letter: God's power shows itself in his servants' weakness.

The smell may come from the same picture, the incense of the parade. It may also recall the sacrifices of the temple, whose smoke rose to God as a pleasing aroma. To the same people, the same smell meant life or death. So does the message of Christ.

‘Peddle’ is the Greek kapēleuō. The kapēlos was a small trader, often a wine seller, and such traders had a name for watering down their goods and cheating. Travelling speakers who taught for money were common in the Greek cities. Paul says he does not sell the gospel, and he does not water it down.
passages.ot:
The ‘pleasing aroma’ is an Old Testament phrase. Of a burnt offering the law says, “it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma” (Exodus 29:18). After the flood, “the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma” of Noah's offering (Genesis 8:21). God promised through Ezekiel that he would accept his gathered people themselves “as a pleasing aroma” (Ezekiel 20:41).

‘Those who are being saved and those who are perishing’ recalls Moses' choice set before Israel: “See, I have set before you today life and goodness, as well as death and disaster” (Deuteronomy 30:15).

‘Who is qualified for such a task?’ is a question Moses also felt. When God sent him, he answered, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant” (Exodus 4:10). Paul will soon answer his own question: “our competence comes from God” (3:5).

And the picture of watered-down goods is in Isaiah too. The prophet says of a faithless city, “your fine wine is diluted with water” (Isaiah 1:22).
passages.asks: Paul left an open door because he could not rest without news of his friends. Ask what that says about how much people mattered to him. Then ask whether you are ever tempted to ‘water down’ the message of Christ to make it easier to sell. And ask whether you would be willing, like Paul, to be seen as a captive in someone else's victory.
